summary.text: A woman in her early 50s with rheumatoid arthritis, taking oral methotrexate and methylprednisolone for the past two months, presented with a 3-day history of epigastric pain, nausea, recurrent non-bilious vomiting and passage of black stools. She had pallor, non-blanching purpuric lesions on the lower extremities and mild epigastric tenderness without a palpable mass.

Hemoglobin was 6.6 g/dL with raised C-reactive protein and sedimentation rate, and liver, kidney, coagulation, amylase and lipase tests were normal. Chest X-ray, ultrasonography and upper endoscopy were unremarkable, and colonoscopy showed clotted blood without a bleeding source. CT angiography showed a 17x15 mm saccular outpouching with surrounding hematoma, identified on 3D reconstruction as a right colic artery pseudoaneurysm, with rheumatoid vasculitis suggested as the cause.

She was resuscitated with intravenous fluids and other drugs and received three units of packed red blood cells. After normal hemoglobin levels were achieved, selective SMA angiography localized the pseudoaneurysm, and transarterial coil embolization with titanium micro-coils of the right colic artery and a collateral SMA branch produced complete occlusion. An intravenous corticosteroid and oral methotrexate were started for the vasculitis.

The procedure led to symptom resolution: abdominal pain was relieved within two days of conservative treatment, vomiting subsided and an oral diet was tolerated, with hemoglobin 12 g/dL and no recurrence of bleeding. She was discharged in stable condition on day 4 post-procedure and was asymptomatic and doing well at the two-month follow-up.
